extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, advocates, and organizations submitting comments on agency rulemaking (especially environmental rulemaking)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting effective written public comments to federal (and state) agency rulemakings, focused on making arguments relevant, readable, evidence-based, and actionable for agency staff. Geared especially toward environmental rulemaking but applicable more broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether submitting a public comment is the right action
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if a public comment is the best way to influence agency action versus other engagement options (public meetings, providing information, contacting legislators, responding to guidelines or plans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider other participatory routes (public meetings, agency requests for information, legislative pressure, Unified Agenda contacts) and use resources (e.g., 'Beyond Public Comments: Other Ways to Engage With and Influence Federal Agencies') to choose the most appropriate method for your goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide specific arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid broad, conceptual comments that do not address particulars of the proposed rule; target specific provisions and provide a rationale and evidence for your positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad comments often receive little consideration. Explicitly tie statements to parts of the proposal and explain why the agency should accept or change a particular element. Anti-pattern: submitting general statements of support or opposition without linking to the rule text or providing reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide original arguments or data (technical and/or legal rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer arguments, analyses, or evidence the agency has not already considered, including technical or legal rationale that adds new information to the docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies prioritize novel information. If you can supply unique data, alternative analyses, or legal interpretations not in the proposal's record, your comment is more likely to influence the outcome. Avoid repeating arguments already thoroughly addressed in the rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure arguments are directly relevant to the proposed rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep content focused on issues that bear on the rule at hand; irrelevant topics may be ignored or not read by relevant staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce unrelated issues (e.g., discussing labor issues in a comment about effluent standards). Relevance increases the chance agency staff will consider and respond to your points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include data and analyses to support claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, attach or cite data, statistical analyses, or methodological evidence that underpin your claims about the rule’s impacts or correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the proposed rule’s supporting analyses (e.g., Regulatory Impact Analysis, Integrated Science Assessment) to check assumptions and identify gaps. Well-documented data and reproducible analyses strengthen credibility. If data are not online, host them on an accessible site or attach files in accessible formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your comment clear and easy to read
rubrics_metrics.description: Write plainly and structure your comment so non-expert screeners (contractors or software) and agency staff can quickly understand key points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies often use contractors and specialized software to sort comments; these readers may not be subject-matter experts, so avoid subtlety that won’t survive automated or non-expert review. Use clear organization, headings, and concise language to prevent nuance from being lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly identify the rule section(s) addressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state which section(s) of the proposed rule your comment pertains to at every relevant point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Federal Register's labels and linking features, type in section numbers, or paste the agency's questions from the proposed rule to make it easy for reviewers to map your comment to the rule text. Repeating the targeted section helps ensure your point is associated with the correct part of the docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include properly formatted references and accessible supporting materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite sources so agency staff can find them easily, and provide access to any underlying data or documents you rely on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format references clearly (full citations, URLs). If referenced data are not readily accessible online, either host them on a publicly accessible website you cite or attach data files in accessible formats to the docket. Agencies value information they have not already considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your comment stand out (but be wary of mass-letter limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for distinctiveness and substantive content; mass-generated template comments are often counted as a single comment and less likely to change technical rule details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass letter campaigns can raise public awareness but typically have limited influence on specific regulatory text because agencies may treat them collectively. To increase impact, personalize or add substantive, site-specific, or technical points rather than only signing a form letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact agency staff for clarification when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed rule or docket materials are unclear, reach out to the agency contact listed in the proposed rule or the Unified Agenda for questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency staff can clarify scope, data sources, or procedural questions that will help you craft a more precise and useful comment. Use the listed contact rather than guessing or misinterpreting technical details.
